title: The CLI in CI/CD
summary: Inject vault secrets into any process with env pull, push, and run, using ONECLAW_TOKEN and ONECLAW_VAULT_ID in CI.

blocks.text: In a pipeline you don't want secrets committed to a repo or pasted into CI settings one by one. The CLI pulls them from a vault at runtime and injects them into your process.
In CI, authenticate with env vars instead of 1claw login: set ONECLAW_TOKEN (a JWT) or ONECLAW_API_KEY, plus ONECLAW_VAULT_ID for the vault to read.

steps.text: Set the non-interactive credentials in your shell or CI secrets store. Exchange your 1ck_ key at POST /v1/auth/api-key-token (see Foundations), or use your 1ck_ key directly as ONECLAW_API_KEY. Use the vault UUID from `1claw vault list` or from the Foundations track.
Seed your vault with a local .env file first.
Pull secrets into a .env file for tooling that reads one.
Or skip the file entirely and run a command with secrets injected as env vars. This is the safest option since nothing lands on disk.

blocks.text: CLI env commands (env push, env pull, env run) require @1claw/cli v0.38+. If you see errors on v0.37.x, use the API directly: curl -X PUT https://api.1claw.co/v1/vaults/$ONECLAW_VAULT_ID/secrets/config/env -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"type":"env_bundle","value":"KEY=value\nKEY2=value2"}'

blocks.caption: GitHub Actions step that pulls secrets from the vault

blocks.text: For offline or flaky-network builds, run 1claw env cache to store secrets in a local AES-256-GCM encrypted file (default TTL 300s). env run uses a valid cache automatically; add --no-cache to bypass it.
Your build process now starts with secrets injected straight from the vault, with no plaintext secrets checked into the repo or pasted into CI config.
Where this goes wrong in practice. CI is the place secrets leak most often, because a pipeline is a machine that prints things for a living.

items: Values reach the log. Any step that echoes an environment, runs with set -x, or dumps a failed request body publishes the secret to anyone who can read the build. The official GitHub Action emits ::add-mask:: before export for exactly this reason.
Pull requests from forks inherit the workflow. A deny-by-default ref list is what stops an untrusted branch from running a job that can read your vault.
One CI credential is shared by every job. Convenient, and it means the smallest job on the least trusted branch holds the same access as the deploy.

The key is stored in CI and forgotten. A key in a CI secret store is a key with no expiry in a system many people can configure, which is why the agent key should be exchanged for a short-lived token at job start rather than used directly.
Caches and artifacts outlive the job. A .env written for a build step and left in a cached directory is available to every subsequent run.

blocks.text: Assume the build log is public even when the repository is private. Logs get pasted into issues, forwarded to vendors and attached to support tickets more often than anyone plans for.

blocks.situation: A workflow needs one secret during a deploy step. A colleague adds it to the job-level env block so any step can use it, arguing that scoping it per step is fussy.
blocks.question: What is the practical objection?

options.text: Job-level env is slower because it is resolved for every step.
options.feedback: Resolution cost is negligible and arguing efficiency loses the point. The objection is about exposure, not performance.

options.text: Every step in the job now has the value in its environment, including third-party actions you did not write.
options.feedback: Correct. A job typically runs several actions from other people, and job-level env hands the secret to all of them. Step-level scoping means only the step that needs it can see it.

options.text: Job-level env values are written to the build log automatically.
options.feedback: They are not logged automatically. Masking exists precisely because values reach logs by accident rather than by default.

options.text: It prevents the value from being masked.
options.feedback: Masking works at either scope. The difference is how many steps hold the value, not whether it can be redacted.

quiz.question: Which command runs a process with vault secrets injected as env vars and nothing written to disk?
quiz.explanation: env run injects the values into a child process and writes nothing to disk, so there is no file to forget to delete and nothing left in a cached workspace between runs.

quiz.question: Which two env vars typically authenticate and scope the CLI in CI?
quiz.explanation: ONECLAW_TOKEN (or ONECLAW_API_KEY) authenticates and ONECLAW_VAULT_ID scopes vault commands. Prefer a short-lived token over a long-lived key here: CI is a system many people can configure.

quiz.question: What does 1claw env cache store secrets in?
quiz.explanation: AES-256-GCM in a local file, so env run keeps working when the API is unreachable. It is a real copy of your secrets on that disk, which is worth knowing before you enable it on a shared runner.

concepts.note: scoping a CI credential to the job

title: Lab: leak a secret into a build log
summary: Publish a token to a log and to the process table in four lines, then fix both without changing what the job does.

blocks.text: CI is where secrets leak most often, and almost never through anything exotic. This lab does it two ordinary ways, then closes both. Everything runs locally; no CI provider is involved.

steps.text: Write a job that does something entirely reasonable.
steps.code:
mkdir -p /tmp/cilab && cd /tmp/cilab
cat > job.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
API_TOKEN="sk-live-9f2a-DO-NOT-LEAK"

echo "--- deploying ---"
set -x                    # someone added this to debug a failure
curl -s -o /dev/null "https://example.com/deploy?token=$API_TOKEN" || true
set +x
echo "--- done ---"
EOF
chmod +x job.sh && ./job.sh

steps.text: Read the output. `set -x` echoes each command after expansion, so the token is now in the build log.
Harvest it the way anyone with read access to the log would.
Now the second leak, which people miss entirely. A secret passed as a command-line argument is visible in the process table while the command runs.
steps.code:
python3 -c "import time; time.sleep(4)" --token=sk-live-VISIBLE-IN-PS &
sleep 0.5; ps -o args= -p $!

steps.text: The token is right there in the arguments.
Compare with passing it in the environment instead. Same process, same secret, and nothing in the process table.
steps.code:
API_TOKEN=sk-live-HIDDEN python3 -c "import time; time.sleep(4)" &
sleep 0.5; ps -o args= -p $!

steps.text: Fix the log leak by redacting known values before anything is printed. This is what ::add-mask:: does in GitHub Actions and what the official 1Claw action emits before it exports anything.
The command still runs and the value is gone from the output.
Clean up.

blocks.text: Take the two failures separately, because they need different fixes.

items: The log leak is about output, and masking is the answer. It works only for values you have told the masker about, which is why the credential should come from somewhere that knows what it just handed you.
The process-table leak is about invocation, and masking cannot help. The fix is to never put a secret in argv: use an environment variable, a header read from a file, or stdin.

blocks.text: Masking is a backstop, not a boundary. It catches the value it was given and nothing else, so a token that arrives by a path your masker does not know about is printed in full. Prefer not producing the value over redacting it afterwards.
Assume the build log is public even on a private repository. Logs get pasted into issues, forwarded to vendors and attached to support tickets, and none of those paths check who is reading.
Nothing in this lab required a vulnerability. A debugging flag someone forgot to remove, and a credential passed the most obvious way, were enough.

quiz.question: Why did `set -x` leak the token?
options: It echoes each command after variable expansion, so the value appears in the log
It writes the environment to the log
It forces curl into verbose mode
quiz.explanation: Tracing prints the command as it will actually run, with variables already substituted. That is exactly what makes it useful for debugging and what makes it dangerous with secrets.

quiz.question: Why can masking not fix the process-table leak?
options: Masking only works on stdout, and ps reads the kernel's copy of the arguments
ps output is written before masking starts
The mask pattern does not match argv
It can, if the mask is applied earlier
quiz.explanation: Masking filters a stream you control. The process table is read from the kernel by other processes, so the only fix is to keep the secret out of argv entirely.

quiz.question: Which is the more reliable defence?
options: Redacting the value after it is produced
Not producing it: keep it out of argv and out of traced commands
Deleting the build log after each run
quiz.explanation: Masking depends on knowing the value in advance and catching every path it can take. Not emitting it has no such dependency.

title: The TypeScript SDK
summary: Install @1claw/sdk, create a client, and fetch a secret using the {data, error} response envelope.

blocks.text: The SDK gives Node apps and agents typed, full-parity access to the API. Every call returns an envelope so you check for errors without try/catch everywhere.

Auth options when creating a client: a personal API key (apiKey: '1ck_...') for server-side work, agent credentials (agentId + apiKey: 'ocv_...') which the SDK exchanges for a JWT and refreshes automatically, or manual login.

steps.text: Install the SDK in a Node 20+ project.
Set your key and vault ID in the environment so they stay out of source. Use your vault UUID from `1claw vault list`.

Write a script that creates a client and fetches a secret. Check res.error before using res.data. Use a path that exists in your vault, such as `api-keys/openai` from Foundations. Create one with `1claw secret set` if needed. Save the code above as `fetch-secret.ts`.
Run it.

blocks.text: Every method returns { data, error, meta }. Typed error classes like AuthError (401), NotFoundError (404), and RateLimitError (429) are exported from @1claw/sdk if you prefer to switch on the type.
You have a running script that authenticates with the SDK and prints a fetched secret value. That's the foundation for any Node service or agent that needs vault access.
Where this goes wrong in practice. The SDK is a thin client over the API, and most problems come from treating its return values casually.

items: The response envelope is ignored. Every call resolves to { data, error, meta }, so destructuring domain fields directly yields undefined rather than throwing, and the bug surfaces somewhere unrelated.
Errors are assumed to be exceptions. A 402 payment-required or an approval-required response arrives as a value in error, not as a rejected promise, and a try/catch alone will not see it.
The client is constructed per request. It is designed to be long-lived and to manage token exchange and refresh; rebuilding it per call re-authenticates constantly and defeats that.
Secret values are logged during debugging. A console.log of a whole response object prints the value, and that line survives into production more often than anyone admits.

blocks.text: Check error before reading data on every call. It is more verbose than optimistic destructuring and it is the difference between a clear failure and a silent undefined.

quiz.question: What shape does every SDK method return?
options: A Promise that throws on any non-200
quiz.explanation: Every call resolves to { data, error, meta } rather than throwing. That means a 402 or an approval-required response arrives as a value in error, so a try/catch alone will not see it: check error before reading data.

quiz.question: How do you construct a client for server-side work with a personal key?
quiz.explanation: createClient takes baseUrl and a 1ck_ personal key for human or server-side work. Construct it once and keep it: it is designed to be long-lived and manages token exchange for you.

quiz.question: When you pass agentId + apiKey (ocv_) to createClient, what does the SDK handle for you?
options: Exchanging credentials for a JWT and refreshing it before expiry
quiz.explanation: With agent credentials the SDK performs the exchange and refreshes before expiry, so your code holds an identity rather than a bearer token. That is why the client should be long-lived rather than rebuilt per request.

title: Versioning and Rotation
summary: Rotate secrets server-side or with a client-supplied value, list version history, and disable old versions.

blocks.text: Every write to a path creates a new version and keeps the old ones. You can rotate in two ways: PUT a new value yourself, or have the vault generate a random one server-side so the plaintext never touches your client.

items: Client-supplied: PUT a new value to the same path, creating a new version
Server-side: POST to secret-rotate, the vault generates and stores the value
List: GET secret-versions returns all versions newest first with is_disabled
Disable: a disabled version is kept for audit but reads return 410 Gone

steps.text: Set your credentials. Use your 1ck_ key directly as a Bearer token, or exchange it at POST /v1/auth/api-key-token for a JWT (see Foundations). CLI steps assume you completed `1claw login` from the Install the CLI lesson.
Create the secret you will rotate. Skip this if it already exists from Foundations.
Rotate with a client-supplied value by PUTting a new value to the same path. This creates a new version.
Or rotate server-side. The vault generates a random 32-char hex value and stores it as the next version. You never see or send the plaintext.
Or do the same from the CLI.
List versions to confirm a new one exists.
Disable an old version so any read of it returns 410 Gone. Pick the oldest non-disabled version number from the list output above and use it in place of `1`.

blocks.text: For AI agents, the MCP tools mirror this: rotate_generate creates a random value server-side, rotate_and_store persists a value the agent already regenerated, and list_versions shows history with [disabled] markers.

You've rotated a secret to a fresh version and listed its history. Consumers reading the latest version pick up the new value automatically, and old versions can be disabled without losing the audit trail.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Rotation is straightforward to perform and easy to sequence wrongly, and the wrong order causes an outage rather than a warning.

items: The old version is disabled before consumers move. Rotation creates a new version and leaves the old one readable so both can coexist. Disabling immediately is what turns a rotation into an incident.
Nobody knows who consumes the secret. Rotation is safe when you can enumerate the readers and unsafe when you cannot, and the audit log is the only reliable source for that list.
Server-side generation is skipped. Generating a value yourself means it exists in your shell history, your clipboard and possibly your terminal scrollback before it ever reaches the vault.
Rotation is treated as an incident response only. A credential rotated only after a suspected leak has no established procedure at the moment it is needed most.
Disabling is confused with deleting. Disabling a version is reversible and preserves the record; deleting the key material is cryptographic erasure.

blocks.text: The safe sequence is write the new version, move consumers, verify with the audit log that nothing reads the old one, then disable it. Skipping the verification step is how the last consumer discovers rotation at 3am.

blocks.situation: You rotate a database password server-side. Two hours later a background worker starts failing to connect, and it is the only consumer you had not accounted for.
blocks.question: What is the immediate fix, and what is the durable one?

options.text: Re-enable the old version so the worker recovers, then find and update it.
options.feedback: Correct as the immediate step, and the durable fix follows from why it worked: the old version was still there to re-enable. The lasting change is enumerating consumers from the audit log before rotating rather than after.

options.text: Roll the password back to its previous value in the database.
options.feedback: Now the vault and the database disagree, and every consumer you did update breaks instead. Changing the upstream system to match a stale credential inverts the problem.

options.text: Update the worker's configuration and restart it.
options.feedback: This is the right end state and the wrong first move: it leaves the worker failing while you locate and deploy the change. Restore service first, then fix properly.

options.text: Disable the new version so all consumers fall back to the old one.
options.feedback: Disabling the new version leaves the updated consumers pointing at something unreadable, converting one broken worker into several.

quiz.question: What's the key benefit of server-side rotation over a client PUT?
options: The generated plaintext is never sent to or returned from the client
quiz.explanation: Server-side rotation generates the value in the vault, so the plaintext never touches the client.

quiz.question: What does a read of a disabled version return?
quiz.explanation: 410 Gone rather than 404, and the distinction is deliberate: the version existed and was deliberately retired. Disabling is reversible and preserves the record, unlike destroying the key material.

quiz.question: Which MCP tool stores a value an agent already regenerated?
quiz.explanation: rotate_and_store persists a value the agent already has; rotate_generate has the server produce one. Prefer server-side generation where you can, since a value you generate first exists in your shell history and clipboard.

concepts.note: persistence: why a key with no expiry is a standing risk

title: Environment variables and bundles
summary: Use first-class per-key env vars with production/preview/development scoping, and know when the older env_bundle secret still fits.

blocks.text: Since v0.51, 1Claw stores environment variables as first-class per-key entries on a vault, with Vercel-style environment scoping. Each entry targets a specific environment (production, preview, development, or a custom one you define), and is encrypted individually. This replaced the older pattern of stuffing everything into a single env_bundle secret.

items: Vault-level vars live in the vault's env_vars store, addressed by KEY plus environment.
Org-level shared vars can be linked to many vaults at once, so a value like SENTRY_DSN is defined once.
Branch overrides let a preview deployment on feat/checkout get a different value than other previews.
Precedence is three-tier and always resolves in the same order: shared < vault < branch override.
Sensitive write-only mode makes a value non-readable after creation, even for humans.

blocks.text: Vault-level vars with the same KEY and environment always beat org-level shared vars. That is the whole conflict rule; there is no priority field to reason about.

steps.text: Create a vault-scoped variable for production.
Add a different value for preview, so preview deploys never touch the production database.
Resolve the final KEY=VALUE set for an environment. This is what a deploy or a runtime actually consumes.
Resolve with a branch override applied. If a branch-scoped value exists for feat/checkout it wins; otherwise you get the plain preview value.
Do the same from the CLI, which is what you would use in a deploy script. `env add` takes the key and the environment as positional arguments and prompts for the value.
steps.code:
1claw env ls
1claw env add DATABASE_URL production   # value is prompted
1claw env environments ls

blocks.text: An agent connected over MCP calls the resolve_env tool to get the same resolved set, subject to its policies. It never sees values from an environment it is not scoped to.

The older approach, one env_bundle secret holding many KEY=VALUE lines, still works and still has a place. Use it when you want the whole set to move as a single versioned, rotatable unit, or when a consumer only knows how to read one secret. Reach for per-key env vars whenever you need environment scoping, shared org values, or branch overrides.

blocks.code:
# Legacy / single-unit pattern, still supported
cat .env | 1claw secret set app/env --type env --stdin
1claw env run -- node server.js
blocks.caption: The env_bundle pattern: one secret, one version, injected as a process environment

blocks.text: Cloud Runtimes merge resolved env vars into the container environment at start and rebuild. The combined set is capped at 64KB and a change needs a restart to take effect.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Environment variables feel like configuration rather than secrets, and they get handled accordingly.

items: Precedence is guessed. Resolution is shared, then vault, then branch override, and a value that appears not to apply is nearly always being shadowed by a more specific one rather than missing.
Sensitive mode is applied after the fact. A write-only value cannot be read back, so marking an existing variable sensitive removes your ability to verify what it holds.
The 64KB runtime limit is discovered at deploy. Resolved variables are merged into the container environment at start, and exceeding the cap fails the start rather than truncating quietly.
A restart is assumed unnecessary. Injection happens at start and rebuild, so a changed variable does nothing until the runtime is restarted.
Branch overrides accumulate. An override created for one feature branch stays after the branch is deleted, and later previews inherit a value nobody remembers setting.

blocks.text: When a variable resolves to something unexpected, read the resolve endpoint rather than reasoning about it. It returns the final set with precedence already applied, which is faster than guessing which tier won.

quiz.question: A vault defines DATABASE_URL for production, and an org-level shared var also defines DATABASE_URL for production. Which value wins?
options: The request fails with a conflict error
quiz.explanation: Precedence is shared < vault < branch override. A vault-level var with the same key and environment always beats the org-level shared var.

quiz.question: What does the git_branch query parameter add to an env-vars resolve call?
options: It creates a new environment named after the branch
It applies a branch override on top of the environment's values
It filters results to vars created on that branch
It is only used for audit logging
quiz.explanation: Branch overrides are the top tier of precedence, letting one feature-branch preview differ from other previews without defining a whole new environment.

quiz.question: When is the older env_bundle secret still the better fit?
options: When you want the whole set to version and rotate as one unit
It is deprecated and should never be used
When you need org-level shared values
quiz.explanation: env_bundle is not deprecated. It is the right tool when the set should move as a single versioned unit, or when the consumer can only read one secret. Per-key env vars are the choice when you need scoping, sharing, or branch overrides.

concepts.note: scoping by environment is an ABAC condition

title: Agent environment tagging
summary: Tag an agent as production or preview so its token, its policies, and its env var resolution all agree.

blocks.text: An agent can carry a named environment tag: production, preview, development, or a custom one. The tag is not a label for humans to read. It flows into the agent's JWT as an environment claim, it can gate policies, and it can drive env var resolution automatically.

items: environment: the tag itself.
environment_locked: once set at bootstrap it cannot be changed, so a production agent cannot be quietly relabelled.
env_auto_resolve: the resolve endpoint fills in the environment from the agent's tag instead of trusting a query parameter.
per_environment_guardrails: JSON overrides so the same agent definition enforces tighter limits in production.

blocks.text: Requires: an agent you can update, and a vault with env vars from the previous lesson.

steps.text: Create an agent tagged for production, locked so the tag cannot drift.
Confirm the tag landed. The JWT the agent exchanges for will now carry an environment claim.
Scope a policy to environments with the environment_in condition. This policy only grants access when the calling principal is tagged production.
Resolve env vars as the agent. Because env_auto_resolve is on, you omit the environment parameter entirely: the server uses the agent's tag.

blocks.text: Turn on the org setting env.enforce_agent_environment_scope to block agents from resolving variables outside their tagged environment. Without it, a preview-tagged agent can still ask for production values if a policy allows it.
The payoff is that one mistake stops being possible: a preview agent cannot read production values, because the environment is fixed in its identity rather than supplied per request.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Tagging is easy to adopt and easy to adopt decoratively, which is worse than not adopting it.

items: Tags are set without enforcement. Without env.enforce_agent_environment_scope an agent can still resolve variables outside its tag, so the label documents intent without constraining anything.
The tag is left unlocked on production agents. environment_locked is immutable only if you set it, and an unlocked production tag can be edited to development to widen access.
env_auto_resolve is left off. With it off the environment comes from a caller-supplied query parameter, which is exactly the value an attacker would choose.
Per-environment guardrails are configured once and diverge. Overrides per environment are powerful and become the place where production quietly ends up looser than preview.

blocks.text: The whole value of tagging is that the environment comes from identity rather than from a request. Every one of these failures gives that back.

quiz.question: Why does env_auto_resolve improve safety over passing ?environment=production?
options: It encrypts the resolved values in transit
It caches the resolved values for faster reads
The environment comes from the agent's identity instead of a caller-supplied parameter
It allows the agent to read every environment at once
quiz.explanation: A query parameter is supplied by the caller and can be changed. With env_auto_resolve the server reads the environment from the agent's own tag, so the agent cannot ask for a different one.

quiz.question: What does environment_locked prevent?
options: Changing the agent's environment tag after bootstrap
The agent reading any environment variables
quiz.explanation: environment_locked makes the tag immutable after bootstrap, so a production-scoped identity cannot later be relabelled as development to widen its access.

quiz.question: Which org setting stops a preview-tagged agent from resolving production variables?
quiz.explanation: env.enforce_agent_environment_scope blocks resolution outside the agent's tag. env.require_sensitive_prod is a different setting that forces prod and preview vars to be write-only.
